title: Navigation for a logistics company
metaTitle: Logistics navigation as a job map
excerpt: Label the menu with jobs an operator already has words for, and make one path request a quote. Department names and industry lists force a translation nobody came to do.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it, sorting the paths before they become a menu.
caption: A stylus over wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside the tablet. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in a logistics site header?
faqs.answer: A way to request a quote, a way to see rates or accessorials, a way to track an existing number, and a way to read one real move. Five to seven items is enough. Put careers, press, and one-off campaigns in the footer or cut them. The quote label should match the button on the homepage.

faqs.question: Should we list every industry we serve?
faqs.answer: Only when the industry changes the work, such as temperature or appointments, and then say that change. Six pages that repeat one paragraph with a noun swapped are not navigation. They compete with quote, track, and claims, which are the jobs people actually came to do.

faqs.question: How is Request a quote different from Track?
faqs.answer: Quote is for someone deciding whether you get the freight. Track is for someone who already has a reference number. Sending a new shipper into a portal login, or burying the quote under a menu named Solutions, mixes the two jobs. Keep both visible, and do not give them the same emphasis.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
The logistics company website navigation is a map of jobs, not a list of departments. An operator who needs to know you can move the thing should see labels they already use, and one path should request a quote. If the menu sounds like an org chart, they have to translate it before they can act. They will not.

Write the jobs on paper before you touch the header.

## Jobs, not departments

The jobs are concrete. Request a quote. See what a rate includes. Read how a mode runs. Track a number you already have. Start a claim. Those can be navigation items. "Solutions," "Industries," "Insights," and "Company" are drawers. An operator with a ready date does not open drawers for sport.

The W3C WCAG overview groups accessibility into four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A menu is operable when it can be used without a precise hover and without a mouse, and understandable when the same job keeps the same name. A mega-menu that reveals different labels on hover, or that calls the quote path three different things, fails both in ordinary use.

Put "Request a quote" in the header with those words, matching the homepage button. Do not let it become "Get a rate," "Talk to sales," and "Start" in three places. One door, one name.

Five to seven items is enough, especially on a phone in a yard. Extra pages go to the footer, grouped by job, or they wait until someone asks twice. A menu cloned from a global integrator will make a regional carrier look evasive. Evasive is an expensive look when the freight is time-sensitive.

## Words they already use

Take labels from the phone, from emails, and from bills of lading. Quote, track, POD, claims, accessorials, equipment. If your market says "rate" and not "pricing," use rate in the menu and in the page title. Consistency beats the prettier synonym.

Read the list, with no design, to someone who books freight. Ask where they would click to price a load, where they would click if a receiver refused it, and where they would click to see a real move. Hesitation means the label is internal. Change the label.

Applicants, brokers, and shippers may share a site and not a vocabulary. Do not average them into "partners." Give drivers a plain item if you hire drivers, and do not style it like the quote button. The quote is the commercial door. Careers can be found. It should not win the header by shouting.

"Industries we serve" is the usual way a menu avoids words. A page that repeats the same paragraph with "retail," "automotive," and "food" swapped in is not six jobs. If an industry changes the work, say the change: temperature, appointments, floor-loaded freight. If it does not, you do not need the item.

## One path that requests a quote

The quote item goes to the same place from every page. A short form with the facts a desk needs, or a clear checklist, not a marketing page that asks them to pick a persona. Tracking goes to tracking. Sign-in, if you have a portal, is for people who already have an account. Do not send a new shipper into a password field.

Campaign pages can emphasize a mode. The global header should stay stable. A header that rearranges itself by audience will rearrange itself by accident, and a regular who tenders every week will lose the path they memorized. Stability is part of being understandable.

On a phone, the quote action should be visible without nesting it under "More." If the condensed menu hides the only commercial door, promote it and demote a department. The yard is a worse place to hunt than the office, and a lot of this traffic is in the yard.

Check the button on the pricing page, the service blocks, and the proof pages. Same sentence, same destination. A navigation project that updates the header and leaves "Contact sales" on the rate card has not finished.

## Where proof and price sit in the map

Give skeptics a label they would actually tap. "Rates and accessorials" beats "Transparent pricing." "A load we held for the window" beats "Case studies," if that is the true story. Pick one phrase and use it in the menu, the title, and the first heading.

Google's guidance on title links asks for titles that describe the page and that are not a repeated block of boilerplate. If the menu says "Rates" and the title says "Acme | Logistics redefined | Rates," the tab and the search result waste the only label the operator sees. "Rates and accessorials" is enough. The brand can sit in its usual place without eating the front of every title.

Proof belongs in the map if you are using it to win freight. A footer item called "Resources" is where those stories go to be unread. Name the lane or the mode. Secondary documents, a tariff PDF, a privacy note, an insurance certificate request, can live in the footer with their own names. Do not bind them into one "Legal" file nobody can quote from.

## The footer is part of the map

Group the footer by job. Quote, rates, modes, claims, track. Then the company facts an accounts payable clerk needs: legal name, remit address, hours. Repeat the quote path once for the person who reached the bottom of a proof page ready to send a lane. Same words. A second line that says "Let's move your supply chain forward" is a different company interrupting.

The logo goes home. It should have an accessible name that is the company name. It should not be the only way to request a quote. Logos are a convention for the homepage. They are a bad convention for the action.

Review the footer when a campaign ends. One-off landing pages accumulate links. A footer that records every promotion stops being a map. Remove the expired lane. Keep the jobs.

## When tracking and quoting share a roof

Many carriers have a portal, a phone line, and a marketing site, and the navigation pretends they are one mood. They are three tools. The public menu should route. Quote goes to the quote path. Track goes to the place a PRO number is typed. The portal login is named "Sign in," not "Get started," so a new shipper does not make an account in order to ask a price.

Do not mirror the portal's settings in the marketing header. Notifications, users, and invoices are jobs for people who already ship with you. A prospect does not need them beside "Rates." If a regular lands on the marketing site out of habit, Sign in is their door, visible and dull on purpose.

Write the map in one list that design and the site both use. When a banner invents a new verb for the same quote form, the list has been ignored, and the page you paid to promote is the page that breaks the habit. Fix the banner. Leave the label alone.

Review the list after a peak season, when temporary pages appeared for a weather event or a lane you added for a month. Remove what ended. A menu is a current description of the desk, not a scrapbook.

## Check it with people who book freight

Sit with a few operators, or with coordinators who do this work, and do not explain the company first. Show the phone header. Ask how they would price a load, how they would track one, and where a real move is described. Write down their words when they get lost. Those words replace your labels. The words you have to define get cut.

Then ask one driver applicant, or one receiver, only to confirm their door exists. You are not trying to give every audience the hero. You are trying not to strand them. If a receiver looking for a delivery window can only find "Request a quote," you will pollute the quote desk with the wrong notes.

Change labels in one pass: header, footer, buttons, titles, and the confirmation email. A new verb on a single banner undoes the map on the page where you spent money to be found.

Before the header ships, print the list and the live pages side by side. Every item must land on a page whose first heading repeats the label, or comes close enough that a tired coordinator would agree it is the same job. A menu item that opens a manifesto has failed, even if the URL is pretty.

Tab through the header with a keyboard. The quote path should be reachable, visible when focused, and not dependent on a hover that a phone cannot do. This is the operable half of the menu, and it is also how you notice items that only exist as tiny gray type on a photograph.

Ask the person who answers the phone to read the menu aloud once. If they stumble or translate, the site will stumble in the same place. Change the word while the change is still a line in a file, not a pattern in twenty banners.

The pictures have to match the labels. A menu can say "a held trailer" while the photography is still a container on the water. That gap is [photography direction for a logistics company](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-logistics-company).

When you want the map sorted before the header is redrawn, start with [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services).
